nature-econ-315.title: Profit maximization: where the next unit stops paying
nature-econ-315.text: Every firm in a standard textbook wants one thing. Mainstream economics treats the firm as a rational agent that seeks the most profit, meaning total revenue minus total cost. Profit maximization is the process of choosing the price, inputs and output that reach that peak. The answer lies at the margin. Marginal revenue is the extra money from selling one more unit, and marginal cost is the extra cost of making it. As long as marginal revenue is larger, producing more adds profit. Profit peaks where the two are equal. Under perfect competition the firm's demand curve is its marginal revenue curve, a flat line at the market price. Some costs do not change the decision at all. In the short run, a change in overhead such as rent, explored in {{ref:nature-econ-307}}, leaves the best output and price untouched, because those costs are treated as sunk. Where an extra customer costs almost nothing, as with a seat on a scheduled flight, maximizing profit simply means maximizing revenue. The pursuit has limits. Some profit-maximizing behavior harms consumers, and competition law regulates it. And the newer field of {{ref:nature-econ-021}} replaces strict profit maximization with a more limited kind of rationality in its models.

nature-econ-312.title: The production function: from inputs to output
nature-econ-312.text: Give a workshop more workers and more machines, and how much more will it make? A production function answers that question. It is a technical relation showing how much output can be made from given quantities of physical inputs. It is usually read as the maximum output each combination of inputs can give, so it traces a frontier of the possible. Economists write it as Q = f(X1, ..., Xn), where Q is output and the Xs are inputs such as capital, labor, land or raw materials. No inputs means no output. Prices and costs play no part; the function links physical things to physical things. From it economists define the extra output from one more unit of an input, the subject of {{ref:nature-econ-310}}. It also shows how output responds when every input grows together, which {{ref:nature-econ-317}} explores. For whole economies, aggregate production functions split growth into the part that comes from more capital and the part that comes from better technology. The Cobb–Douglas form, first developed in 1927, was the first aggregate production function to be estimated and presented to economists. Not everyone accepts these tools. Some economists reject aggregate production functions outright. A debate from the 1950s to the 1970s, begun by Joan Robinson, questioned how capital can be measured at all. Economists have long argued over whether such functions are valid.

nature-econ-307.title: Fixed costs: the bills that arrive regardless
nature-econ-307.text: A bakery pays the same rent whether its ovens run all day or sit cold. That rent is a fixed cost, also called overhead: a business cost that does not change with how much the business produces. Fixed costs tend to recur, like monthly rent or interest, and are often capital costs. The bakery's phone line is another. Its wages are not, because more bread needs more workers. 'Fixed' has a time limit. Costs stay fixed only for the period a contract sets, and in the long run there are none, because every input can change. Some costs are mixed, such as a phone bill with a fixed charge plus calls. Fixed costs also act as a barrier that keeps new businesses out. Accounting and economics use the terms differently, and in recent years fixed costs have come to exceed the costs that rise with output at many companies.

nature-econ-309.title: The short run and the long run: time in economics
nature-econ-309.text: Time changes what a business can do. In economics the short run is a period when some inputs or prices cannot yet change, while the long run is long enough for everything to adjust fully. Alfred Marshall introduced the distinction in his 1890 Principles of Economics. There is still no hard rule for how long either period lasts. In the short run some inputs are fixed, so only variable inputs such as labor and raw materials can change output. All actual production happens here. A profit-maximizing firm expands output while marginal cost is below marginal revenue and cuts back when it is above. In the long run nothing is fixed. Firms can change their capital, resize their plants, or enter and leave industries in response to profits and losses. That movement pushes them toward the lowest possible cost per unit. Economists who study whole economies use the terms a little differently. For them the long run is when prices, contracted wages and expectations have fully adjusted. Keynes thought economists neglected the short run in favor of that distant horizon. 'In the long run,' he remarked, 'we are all dead.'

nature-econ-317.title: Returns to scale: what happens when you double everything
nature-econ-317.text: Double every worker and machine a firm uses, and what happens to output? Returns to scale is the answer: how much output rises, in proportion, when all inputs grow together in the long run. Constant returns mean output doubles too. Decreasing returns mean it less than doubles, mainly because management and coordination get harder as scale grows. Increasing returns mean it more than doubles, thanks to the efficiency gains of size. One firm can show all three, with increasing returns at low output, constant in between and decreasing at high output. Mainstream theory holds that technology alone sets the pattern, not market conditions. With fixed input prices, constant returns mean flat long-run costs per unit, decreasing returns mean rising ones and increasing returns mean falling ones. For a Cobb–Douglas function, returns are increasing if the exponents sum to more than 1, constant if they sum to 1, and decreasing if less. Increasing returns can also trap whole economies. Path-dependent increasing returns help lock industrial economies into fossil-fuel energy systems.

nature-econ-311.title: Monopolistic competition: many sellers, each a little different
nature-econ-311.text: A street of restaurants is a lesson in economics. Each offers something slightly different, yet each can stand in for the others. This is monopolistic competition: many producers selling products that differ, by brand or quality, so they are not perfect substitutes. Differences may be real or perceived, in style, reputation or location. Cereals, clothing, shoes and city service industries are other textbook cases. Each firm has a little market power. Its demand curve slopes down, so it can raise its price without losing every customer. Entry and exit are free, so any economic profit in the short run shrinks toward zero in the long run. The result is inefficient. Firms charge more than marginal cost and run with spare capacity, below the output where cost per unit is lowest. Variety can raise total utility by meeting people's wants better, while heavy advertising is a common concern. Edward Chamberlin pioneered the theory in his 1933 book, alongside Joan Robinson's work on imperfect competition.

nature-econ-310.title: Marginal product: what one more worker adds
nature-econ-310.text: Add workers to a kitchen of fixed size and output first climbs, then slows, and can finally fall. Each step measures the marginal product. It is the extra output gained by using one more unit of an input, such as one more worker, while other inputs stay the same. The rise-then-fall pattern is general. As more of one input is added to a fixed amount of another, marginal product first rises, then falls, and can turn negative. When total output reaches its peak, marginal product is zero. With inputs that can be divided finely, it is the derivative, or rate of change, of the production function. For labor it is the slope of the total product curve. Neoclassical theory says that in competitive markets the marginal product of labor equals the real wage. Output here is usually measured ignoring external costs and benefits. For capital the idea is disputed. The Cambridge capital controversy showed that capital's marginal product cannot generally equal its return once a model has more than one good.

nature-econ-322.title: The theory of the firm: why businesses exist
nature-econ-322.text: If markets coordinate so well, why do businesses exist at all? The theory of the firm is the set of economic theories that explain and predict the nature of firms such as businesses and corporations. It covers their origin, survival, behavior, structure and relation to the market. Its central puzzle is why not every transaction goes through the market, and where the boundary between firm and market lies. The field took shape around the First World War. Economists then shifted from studying whole industries to single firms, because perfect competition no longer described how firms behaved. Its main frameworks look at the costs of using markets, managerial economics, behavioral theory, the resource-based view and dynamic capabilities. Managerial theories by Baumol, Marris and Williamson suggest managers pursue their own goals, for example maximizing sales once profit satisfies shareholders. Agency theory explains the governance problems that arise when ownership and control are separated.

nature-econ-301.title: Cartels: rivals who agree not to compete
nature-econ-301.text: Rivals who agree to stop competing can make a lot of money, for a while. A cartel is a group of independent firms that agree not to compete so as to raise their profits and dominate a market. Cartels raise prices by creating artificial shortages, through low production quotas, stockpiling and marketing quotas. A survey of studies put the median cartel price increase over the last 200 years at about 23 percent. International cartels reached 28 percent and domestic ones 18 percent. Yet cartels are inherently unstable. Each member is tempted to cheat, selling below the agreed price or above its quota. Outsiders respond too, producing more, using the good more efficiently or investing in substitutes. Discovered 20th-century cartels lasted on average 5 to 8 years. Oligopolies may form cartels, and OPEC is one of the best-known international ones. Adam Smith thought cartels undesirable because they could limit production and the quality of goods. The US Sherman Act of 1890 was the first enforced law against them. Price fixing is now illegal in more than 140 countries.

nature-econ-328.title: Variable costs: the costs that grow with every unit
nature-econ-328.text: Every shirt a clothing maker produces needs its own cloth and its own labor. Those are variable costs: costs that change as the quantity a business produces changes. Sales commission, labor and raw materials are the common examples. Add up the marginal cost of every unit made and the total is the variable cost. Add fixed costs to that and the result is total cost. Some costs straddle the line. Electricity often comes as a fixed standing charge plus a charge for use, which makes it semi-variable. The time horizon matters too. Whether a cost is fixed or variable depends on how far ahead one looks, and over five years all costs can become variable. Nor is every variable cost a direct cost: variable manufacturing overhead is indirect.

nature-econ-299.title: Average cost: what each unit really costs
nature-econ-299.text: A factory built for a set output is cheapest to run at that output. Below it, equipment sits idle; above it, bottlenecks build. The measure behind that pattern is average cost, or unit cost: total cost divided by the number of units produced. It weighs heavily in how businesses decide what price to charge. A typical short-run average cost curve is shaped like a U. At first, fixed costs are spread over more units, so the average falls. Then diminishing returns push marginal costs up and drag the average with them. The rule linking the two is simple. When marginal cost is below average cost, the average falls; when it is above, the average rises. So the rising marginal cost curve crosses average cost at its lowest point. Average fixed cost keeps falling toward zero as output grows. Where fixed costs are high and marginal cost is constant, as in hydroelectric generation, average cost slopes down continuously toward marginal cost. Supplying goods at the lowest possible average total cost is the mark of {{ref:nature-econ-200}}.

nature-econ-318.title: Technological change: how new ways of making things spread
nature-econ-318.text: Fuel cells get cheaper every year. That steady decline is technological change at work: the overall process of inventing, innovating and spreading new technologies or processes. It covers invention, commercialization, research and development, continual improvement and diffusion through industry or society. Economists put it more narrowly, as a change in the set of feasible production possibilities. The old picture was a straight line from laboratory to market. That linear model has largely given way to one with innovation at every stage of research, development, diffusion and use. Improvement is often modeled as a learning curve of falling costs. How models treat it has shifted too. Models of the climate and other systems once treated technological change as coming from outside; now they more often treat it as something policy can influence. Markets give it direction. In market economies profit is a powerful driver, so technologies that meet social needs but promise little profit may never reach the market. And efficiency does not always save resources. As {{ref:nature-eecon-163}} explains, efficiency improvements can raise rather than lower total use of a resource.

nature-econ-302.title: Cournot competition: rivals choosing how much to make
nature-econ-302.text: In 1838 Antoine Augustin Cournot described a market with just two suppliers of spring water. His model became Cournot competition: a model of an oligopoly in which firms compete by each choosing, at the same time, how much to produce. The firms sell an identical product, and each firm's output affects the price. Each takes its rivals' quantities as given, looks at the demand left over, and acts like a monopolist on that remainder. The price settles where demand equals the total quantity all firms produce. The resting point, where no firm wants to change its output, was the first use of an idea now known as {{ref:nature-econ-718}}. Prices are lower and quantities higher with two firms than under monopoly. As the number of firms grows, the price keeps falling, approaching marginal cost when firms are infinitely many. Joseph Bertrand objected that rivals would instead undercut each other's prices.

nature-econ-313.title: Can machines replace nature? Resources in production functions
nature-econ-313.text: Standard production functions usually leave natural resources out. Labor and capital go in; the energy and materials that feed them often do not. This debate asks how, or whether, they should be included. Solow and Stiglitz added natural resources, but in a way that let man-made capital fully substitute for them. In that model, enough machines could always make up for lost resources. The economist Georgescu-Roegen called this a 'conjuring trick', because it ignored the physical limits described in {{ref:nature-eecon-118}}. Neither Solow nor Stiglitz replied. Others have tried to put energy in directly. Treating energy as an independent input gives a form like Q = A L^β K^α E^χ, where L is labor, K is capital and E is energy. Later work says this misrepresents how energy affects production. An alternative makes labor and capital themselves depend on energy, written Q = f(L(E), K(E)). The point is physical. If a region cannot get the resources needed to build or maintain its machines, their output eventually falls to near zero. Whether man-made capital can fully replace natural resources remains disputed, with Georgescu-Roegen's challenge still at the heart of the argument.

nature-econ-308.title: Isoquants: many routes to the same output
nature-econ-308.text: A factory can make the same output with many workers and few machines, or few workers and many machines. An isoquant is the curve joining all the combinations of inputs that produce the same quantity of output. Drawn with two inputs such as labor and capital on its axes, it is a level set of the production function, a slice taken at one output. It is the producer's counterpart of an indifference curve, except that output can be measured exactly in physical units. Its slope is the marginal rate of technical substitution, the rate at which one input can replace the other. Because that rate diminishes, isoquants bow toward the origin. Perfect-substitute inputs give straight isoquants; perfect complements give L-shaped ones with a kink at the fixed ratio. The cheapest input mix lies where an isoquant touches an isocost line, a line of equal spending. There the ratio of marginal products equals the ratio of input prices. Two isoquants never cross.

nature-econ-323.title: Why firms exist: Coase's answer
nature-econ-323.text: In his 1937 essay 'The Nature of the Firm', Coase asked a deceptively simple question. Why is all production not carried on by one big firm? His answer was that firms exist because organizing some production inside a firm costs less than coordinating it through market exchange. The costs of using markets, explored in {{ref:nature-econ-641}}, set where a firm ends and the market begins. The essay was one of the first attempts to define the firm in relation to the market. It became the starting point for the economics of outsourcing. It also explains the firm in a way consistent with constant returns to scale, rather than relying on increasing returns. Later economists note that the line between dealings inside a firm and dealings between firms is blurred by in-between forms, such as cooperation between firms.

nature-econ-300.title: Long-run average cost: unit cost when everything can change
nature-econ-300.text: Given enough time, a firm can rebuild itself around any output it chooses. Long-run average cost is the unit cost of producing a given output when every input, including buildings and machinery, can be changed. The firm is assumed to pick the cheapest mix of inputs for each output level. The curve is most often U-shaped. It slopes down where growing bigger cuts unit costs and up where it raises them, effects explored in {{ref:nature-econ-303}}. If input prices do not change with the firm's purchases, falling unit costs come exactly when the production function has increasing returns to scale. Under perfect competition, long-run equilibrium has every firm producing at the curve's lowest point. Sometimes the curve keeps falling indefinitely. Then the biggest firm has a cost advantage, and the industry tends to become a natural monopoly, as in water and electricity supply.

nature-econ-303.title: Economies of scale: why bigger can be cheaper
nature-econ-303.text: Make a vessel bigger and its surface grows with the square of its size, but its volume grows with the cube. That rule, the square–cube law, is one physical root of economies of scale. These are the cost advantages a business gains from operating on a larger scale, so that each unit of output costs less. Put simply, they occur when average costs fall as output increases. Most sources are not physical. Large firms buy in bulk, hire specialized managers, borrow more cheaply and spread advertising costs over more sales. Returns to scale in production add to the effect. Engineers even use a rough rule: capital cost changes with the 0.6 power of the capacity ratio, so a plant with more capacity costs proportionally less to build. The two ideas are easy to confuse. Economies of scale concern a firm's costs, while returns to scale describe how outputs respond to inputs in the production function. Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations (1776) gave the first systematic analysis, through the division of labor. Economies of scale help explain why firms grow large in some industries, and they shape patterns in international trade. They matter for the climate too. Together with learning by doing, they can lower the costs of climate technologies over time.

nature-econ-306.title: Cournot's dilemma: why scale does not always breed monopoly
nature-econ-306.text: If bigger always means cheaper, the first firm to get a good start should swallow its whole trade. Alfred Marshall saw that Cournot's premises implied exactly that. Yet many industries keep numerous firms of different sizes. The puzzle is Cournot's dilemma. Marshall named factors that limit the runaway, such as the deaths of founders. Morroni argues that once knowledge and the organization of transactions are counted, economies of scale do not always lead to monopoly.

nature-econ-304.title: External economies of scale: savings shared by an industry
nature-econ-304.text: Sometimes a firm gets cheaper because its whole industry grows. External economies of scale are cost savings that come from the growth of a whole industry and benefit most or all of its firms, not just one. When new firms enter, average cost falls for all of them, while internal economies help only the single firm that grows. External economies tend to be more common than internal ones. Sraffa disagreed: he argued such economies are rarely met with, and that under perfect competition economies of scale should be excluded.

nature-econ-305.title: Learning and growth economies: getting cheaper with experience
nature-econ-305.text: Experience cuts costs. Learning and growth economies are dynamic economies of scale that come from the process of growing and from practice, rather than from size itself. Learning by doing improves skills and brings small innovations that steadily lower average costs. These learning economies rise with cumulative production, a pattern called the experience curve. Growth economies are different. They arise when expanding lets a firm use resources or skills it had not fully used.

nature-econ-316.title: The marginal revenue product rule: when to hire one more
nature-econ-316.text: Should a firm hire one more worker? The marginal revenue product rule says yes, as long as that worker brings in at least what they cost. Formally, a firm maximizes profit by using more of an input until the extra revenue it brings equals the input's extra cost. The marginal revenue product is the change in total revenue for each unit change in the input. For labor the rule is written MRP_L = MC_L: the marginal revenue product of labor equals its marginal cost.

nature-econ-314.title: Stages of production: the phases of adding inputs
nature-econ-314.text: Adding more of one input to a fixed plant passes through distinct phases. Economists divide a production function into three stages, according to how output per unit of the variable input changes. In stage 1, output per unit of the variable input rises to a peak. A price-taking firm, one too small to move the market price, always produces beyond this stage. In stage 2 output still rises, but at a decreasing rate, with average and marginal product both falling.

nature-econ-325.title: Asset specificity: when assets are tied together
nature-econ-325.text: Some assets are valuable together and worth far less apart. Asset specificity is Oliver Williamson's idea that firms exist because some assets are tied to each other and worth much less in any other use. If such assets are owned by different firms, the parties get locked in and bargain at length over the gains from trade. Repeated or long transactions need renegotiating, which raises the costs of dealing further. Bringing the assets into one firm is the way out.

nature-econ-324.title: The behavioral theory of the firm: good enough, not best
nature-econ-324.text: Real managers rarely hunt for the single best answer. The behavioral theory of the firm, developed by Cyert and March, explains how decisions are actually made inside firms, going beyond neoclassical economics. It builds on Herbert Simon's idea that limited mental ability lets people be rational only within limits in complex, uncertain situations. People and groups therefore 'satisfice', aiming for realistic goals rather than maximum utility or profit. The neoclassical theory of the firm was not seriously challenged by such managerial and behavioral alternatives until the 1960s.

nature-econ-623.title: Ownership and the hold-up problem: who should own the assets
nature-econ-623.text: Grossman, Hart and Moore built an approach that explains firm boundaries through ownership of assets when contracts are incomplete, unable to spell out every future case. Its seminal works, Grossman and Hart (1986), Hart and Moore (1990) and Hart (1995), built the incomplete contracting paradigm. The logic runs through the hold-up problem. Since deals will be renegotiated, each party expects only part of the return on its investment, and so invests too little. It explains the pros and cons of merging firms, and has been applied to providing shared goods and to privatization.

nature-econ-326.title: The resource-based view: advantage from rare resources
nature-econ-326.text: In 1959 Edith Penrose described a firm as a collection of productive resources. Its growth, she argued, depends on managers finding new uses for resources lying idle. From that argument grew the resource-based view of the firm, developed by Wernerfelt (1984) and Barney (1991). It holds that a firm's lasting competitive advantage comes from resources that are valuable, rare, hard to imitate and not substitutable.

nature-econ-329.title: The shutdown rule: when to keep losing money
nature-econ-329.text: A firm can lose money and still be right to stay open. The shutdown rule says that in the short run a firm should keep producing while its revenue covers its variable costs. If revenue falls short, it should shut down. Fixed costs drop out of the decision, because in the short run they must be paid even at zero output. So a firm earning more than its variable cost but less than its total cost keeps operating. It makes an economic loss, but a smaller one than closing would bring.

nature-econ-319.title: Induced technological change: steering invention with prices
nature-econ-319.text: Make fossil energy relatively more expensive, and invention may turn toward other kinds of energy. Induced technological change is the hypothesis that policymakers can steer the direction of technical progress by changing relative input prices. Climate policy is the standard example. Yet evidence that policy actually induces innovation is still lacking, partly because of long-term policy uncertainty. A related idea, directed technical change, stresses price-driven direction rather than policy-driven scale.

nature-econ-321.title: Neutral technical change: which input does progress favor
nature-econ-321.text: Progress does not lift every input equally. Economists classify technical change by which input's productivity it raises. Hicks-neutral change, named after John Hicks (1932), leaves the ratio of capital's and labor's marginal products unchanged at a given mix of capital and labor. Harrod-neutral change is labor-augmenting, making each worker effectively count for more. Solow-neutral change is capital-augmenting, doing the same for machines.

nature-econ-320.title: Technology diffusion: the S-curve of adoption
nature-econ-320.text: New technologies rarely spread at a steady pace. Technology diffusion is the spread of a technology through a society or industry. It usually follows an S-shaped curve: slow at first, then rapid, then leveling off as the market saturates. Everett Rogers named five attributes that speed acceptance: relative advantage, compatibility, low complexity, trialability and observability. Channels matter too. Mass media mostly build awareness, while face-to-face contact mostly reduces the uncertainty that blocks adoption.

openers.firms-costs-and-market-structure: Every business faces the same puzzle: what price to charge, which inputs to use and how much to make. Economists call the answer profit maximization, the choice that gives the highest possible total profit. This chapter takes that puzzle apart, starting with the technical link between inputs and output and the extra output each added worker brings. It then sorts costs into overhead that stays put and costs that rise with every unit made, and shows how time decides which is which. Along the way it asks why firms exist at all, why some band together to stop competing, and how new technology keeps shifting what can be made.

reviews.firms-costs-and-market-structure: Every idea in this chapter traces back to one choice: the price, inputs and output that make profit as large as possible. The production function sets what is physically possible, while marginal product and returns to scale describe how output responds as inputs grow. Costs turn that into money: fixed and variable costs add up to total cost, average cost traces a U, and in the long run every cost can change and economies of scale can make bigger firms cheaper. Market structure decides how far firms can push prices, from monopolistic competition to Cournot's quantity-setting rivals and outright cartels. Theories of the firm explain why firms exist at all, while technological change keeps moving the frontier of what can be made.
